ne-d3c5354b.stem: If the radial nerve is compressed in the axilla in a patient using crutches incorrectly, what else is seen, unlike a lesion at the radial groove?
options: Weakness of triceps brachii and a reduced triceps reflex
Wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the hand
ne-d3c5354b.explanation: The branches to triceps leave the radial nerve in the axilla and upper arm. In an axillary (crutch) lesion elbow extension is also affected; in a lesion at the shaft of the humerus triceps is usually spared. Both cause wrist drop.

ne-ae42ee32.stem: From which spinal segments does the phrenic nerve arise?
ne-ae42ee32.explanation: 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.' The phrenic nerve is the most important branch of the cervical plexus; C4 makes the main contribution. In spinal cord injuries above C3 spontaneous breathing stops.

ne-adea3654.stem: Where in the spinal cord are the cell bodies of the preganglionic sympathetic neurons?
options: In the dorsal horn of every segment
In the lateral horn of segments T1–L2 (intermediolateral nucleus)
In the anterior horn of segments S2–S4
In the parasympathetic nuclei of the brainstem
In the lateral horn of segments C1–C8
ne-adea3654.explanation: The sympathetic system has a thoracolumbar outflow: the preganglionic neurons lie in the lateral horn of T1–L2 and reach the sympathetic chain through the white rami communicantes. The parasympathetic system is craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4).

ne-d3fdff6f.stem: In which ganglion do the parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland synapse?
ne-d3fdff6f.explanation: The fibres leave the facial nerve in the greater petrosal nerve and reach the pterygopalatine ganglion through the nerve of the pterygoid canal; postganglionic fibres stimulate the gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. This is why VII lesions proximal to the geniculate ganglion cause a dry eye.

ne-41a47503.stem: In which nerve do the parasympathetic fibres that stimulate parotid secretion begin, and in which ganglion do they synapse?
ne-41a47503.explanation: The tympanic branch of IX forms the lesser petrosal nerve; the fibres synapse in the otic ganglion and reach the parotid with the auriculotemporal nerve (V3). The submandibular and sublingual glands are stimulated by the chorda tympani fibres of VII.

ne-196a637e.stem: A long-term smoker has pain radiating to the right shoulder and inner arm, mild ptosis and miosis of the right eye and loss of sweating on the right half of the face. What is the most likely cause?
options: A Pancoast tumour at the right lung apex involving the cervical sympathetic chain
ne-196a637e.explanation: Horner syndrome (ptosis – superior tarsal muscle, miosis – dilator pupillae, anhidrosis) results from damage anywhere along the sympathetic pathway. A tumour of the lung apex involves the stellate ganglion and the lower trunk (C8–T1), causing Horner syndrome and arm pain.

ne-829e615f.stem: Which statement about the sympathetic innervation of the adrenal medulla is correct?
options: The medulla receives no autonomic innervation.
The chromaffin cells are stimulated by postganglionic neurons.
The postganglionic fibres come from the coeliac ganglion.
The preganglionic fibres end directly on the medullary cells; the medulla behaves like a ganglion.
Parasympathetic fibres arrive through the vagus nerve.
ne-829e615f.explanation: The chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla come from the neural crest and are regarded as modified postganglionic neurons. Preganglionic fibres arriving in the splanchnic nerves synapse directly on these cells and stimulate the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline.

ne-86aa969a.stem: Which neurotransmitter is released by the postganglionic fibres in the sympathetic innervation of sweat glands?
ne-86aa969a.explanation: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibres are noradrenergic, but those to the eccrine sweat glands are cholinergic (muscarinic receptors). This is why anticholinergic drugs reduce sweating.

ne-bdaebe1a.stem: Which statement about the pelvic splanchnic nerves is correct?
options: They consist only of sensory fibres.
They carry preganglionic sympathetic fibres from T5–T9.
They are the pelvic branches of the vagus nerve.
They carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from S2–S4.
ne-bdaebe1a.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry the parasympathetic fibres to the bladder (detrusor contraction), rectum, descending and sigmoid colon, and those producing erection ('point'). The thoracic splanchnic nerves (greater T5–T9, lesser T10–T11, least T12) are sympathetic.

ne-f843505f.stem: At the onset of appendicitis the patient describes poorly localised pain around the umbilicus; hours later the pain settles in the right lower quadrant. Why is the initial pain felt around the umbilicus?
options: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the appendix.
The parietal peritoneum is involved early.
The appendix lies just behind the umbilicus.
The visceral afferents of the appendix enter segment T10, and the pain is referred to that dermatome.
ne-f843505f.explanation: Visceral pain from midgut organs is carried with sympathetic fibres to segment T10 and referred to the periumbilical area. When the inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, its somatic innervation localises the pain to McBurney's point.

ne-6eb71b69.stem: Roughly how far along the gut does the parasympathetic supply of the vagus nerve extend?
options: To the left third of the transverse colon (near the left colic flexure)
To the beginning of the sigmoid colon
To the end of the rectum
To the end of the duodenum
To the end of the ileum
ne-6eb71b69.explanation: The vagus supplies derivatives of the foregut and midgut (up to about two thirds of the transverse colon). From the left colic flexure onwards, hindgut derivatives receive their parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).

ne-dd43e180.stem: The stellate ganglion is formed by the fusion of which ganglia?
options: The inferior cervical ganglion and the first thoracic ganglion
The middle cervical and second thoracic ganglia
The superior and middle cervical ganglia
ne-dd43e180.explanation: In most people the stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion forms by fusion of the inferior cervical and T1 ganglia; it lies in front of the neck of the first rib, behind the origin of the vertebral artery. Blocking it is used for sympathetically maintained pain of the upper limb and causes Horner syndrome.

ne-53acb8d2.stem: Which statement about the white rami communicantes is correct?
options: They are found only on spinal nerves T1–L2 and carry myelinated preganglionic fibres.
They are found on all spinal nerves.
They carry parasympathetic fibres to the sympathetic chain.
They are found only on cervical nerves.
ne-53acb8d2.explanation: The white rami look white because the preganglionic fibres are myelinated, and they exist only in segments T1–L2, where the sympathetic outflow is. Grey rami (unmyelinated postganglionic) return from the chain to every spinal nerve, so the vessels, sweat glands and hair muscles of the skin all over the body receive sympathetic fibres.

ne-04a5f34d.stem: Which is the largest commissural fibre bundle connecting the two cerebral hemispheres?
ne-04a5f34d.explanation: The corpus callosum is the largest commissure linking the cortex of the two hemispheres. The internal capsule and corona radiata are projection fibres linking the cortex to lower centres; the fornix is the output pathway of the hippocampus.

ne-7ac85b98.stem: In which gyrus is the primary motor cortex?
ne-7ac85b98.explanation: The primary motor cortex (Brodmann 4) lies in the precentral gyrus just in front of the central sulcus. It initiates voluntary movements of the opposite half of the body; its map is known as the motor homunculus.

ne-2c3b62da.stem: In which gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex?
ne-2c3b62da.explanation: The postcentral gyrus (Brodmann 3, 1, 2) lies just behind the central sulcus and receives touch, pain, temperature and position sense from the opposite half of the body.

ne-9f3ed11f.stem: In which lobe is the primary visual cortex?
ne-9f3ed11f.explanation: The primary visual cortex (Brodmann 17) lies on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, on both sides of the calcarine sulcus. Damage here causes loss of the opposite visual field.

ne-d82e578e.stem: Where is the primary auditory cortex?
options: Transverse temporal gyri (Heschl) on the superior temporal gyrus
ne-d82e578e.explanation: The primary auditory cortex (Brodmann 41–42) lies in the transverse temporal (Heschl) gyri on the surface of the superior temporal gyrus facing the lateral sulcus.

ne-630caf8b.stem: Which sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?
ne-630caf8b.explanation: The central sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes; the motor cortex lies in front of it and the sensory cortex behind it. The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.

ne-e956823f.stem: Which structure is most important for forming new memories?
ne-e956823f.explanation: The hippocampus lies in the medial part of the temporal lobe and plays a key role in transferring short-term memory to long-term memory; bilateral damage leads to inability to form new memories (anterograde amnesia).
